role: Runner script: starts one bwx12 process per spec line and records its exit status.
purpose: rx.sh runs one benchmark process per line of a spec file, on the CPUs 0 to 119. It stores the output of each process as a csv file in a new result folder. It also writes the machine state before the run (`env.txt`) and the launch time and the exit status of each process (`launches.txt`).

main_flow.step: Read the three arguments: the name for the result folder, the path of the binary, the expected sha256.
Stop with exit status 3 when the marker file exists. Stop with exit status 2 when the sha256 of the binary differs.
Create the result folder `w120-<name>-<UTC time>` and write `env.txt`.
For each spec line: test the marker file, wait until at most 2 tasks are runnable (at most 40 s), sleep 5 s, append the `launch` line to `launches.txt`.
Start the binary in the background under `taskset -c 0-119`, with its output in `<tag>.csv`, its error messages in `stderr.txt` and an empty input.
Test once per second whether the process still exists. Kill it and stop with exit status 3 when the marker file appears.
Take the exit status of the process with `wait` and append the `rc` line to `launches.txt`.
After the last spec line: print the result folder, the line count of `launches.txt`, the `rc` lines that are not 0, and the size and the first 600 bytes of `stderr.txt`.

behavior_notes: rx.sh measures nothing itself. It reads no clock for a rate and computes no rate. All timed intervals are inside the binary. The times in `launches.txt` have a step of 1 s and come from `date`.

Exit status of rx.sh: 3 when the marker file exists (lines 7, 13, 19), 2 when the sha256 differs (line 8), otherwise the status of the last command `head` (line 22). A failed binary does not change it. A caller that needs the status of the binary must read the `rc` line. go.sh and go2.sh do this in their function `rxok`.

The wait for at most 2 runnable tasks cannot stop the run. After 40 tries the script starts the process anyway and prints no message. The `launch` line holds `/proc/loadavg` as read after the wait and the 5 s pause.

Thread placement: `taskset -c 0-119` gives the process the CPU list 0 to 119. bwx12 then pins thread i to entry i of its `--cpus` list [Ref3]. Both counts start at 0. The spec lines of the rerun hold `--threads 120 --cpus 0-63,64-119` [Ref2]. So thread i runs on CPU i.

While the binary runs, the shell of rx.sh does three things once per second: it runs `kill -0`, it tests the marker file, and it starts one `sleep 1` process. rx.sh sets no CPU list for its own shell. So these steps run on the CPU list that rx.sh inherited [Ref6]. Under go.sh that list was 0-119 in the rerun [Ref4]. These are the CPUs of the benchmark threads.
Insufficient data: the effect of this once-per-second poll on the measured rates. A comparison run of the same spec line without the poll loop would resolve it.

Insufficient data: the CPU list of rx.sh under go2.sh. go2.sh does not print it [Ref4]. The command lines that started go.sh and go2.sh on CRB hold no `taskset` [Ref9]. The command of go2.sh is the command of go.sh with `go2-T72-` and `go2.sh` in place of `go-T72-` and `go.sh`. A line `taskset -cp $$` in go2.sh would resolve it for a later run.

When the marker file appears during a process, rx.sh kills the process and ends. The csv file of that process then holds only what the binary wrote before the signal. `launches.txt` then holds a `launch` line without an `rc` line.

rx.sh does not record the boot id, MemTotal or the memory speed. `env.txt` holds only the time, the Linux kernel release, the load, the logins, a process list and the binary. go.sh and go2.sh record the boot id and MemTotal in their state lines.

Is the local rx.sh the script that ran in the rerun: go.sh and go2.sh hold the sha256 that rx.sh must have. Each of the two scripts tests the copy of rx.sh on CRB against this value before its first process. It stops the run when the copy differs [Ref10]. Line 20 of the local go.sh was edited on 2026-11-24 (the text of one message). The lines of go.sh that hold this value and its test are the same as in the text that ran [Ref10]. The logs of go.sh and go2.sh hold no line that starts with `FAILED`, and each log ends with `ALLDONE` [Ref11]. The local rx.sh has this sha256 (computed with `sha256sum` on 2026-11-21). So the local rx.sh has the content of the copy that the two scripts tested. The files that rx.sh wrote in the rerun hold no checksum of rx.sh.

What `users` in a `launch` line shows: the number of lines that `who` prints. `env.txt` holds the lines of `who` themselves. go.sh and go2.sh were started through `ssh` (the remote login tool). The two `ssh` connections were open until these scripts ended [Ref9]. In the rerun all 9 `launch` lines show `users 0`, and no `env.txt` holds a line of `who` [Ref12]. So `who` did not list these connections. `users 0` does not show that no connection to CRB was open.

words.def: the Arm reference server under test. It has 128 CPUs.
the whole-chip read test of 2026-11-17, run after the memory speed was lowered from 8000 MT/s to 7200 MT/s.
the two halves of the chip. CPUs 0-63 sit on mesh 0. CPUs 64-127 sit on mesh 1.
our runs use CPUs 0-119 only: 64 threads on mesh 0 plus 56 threads on mesh 1. Each thread reads its own buffer of 256 MiB from memory.
million transfers per second, the unit of memory speed.
later runner programs for the same loops. They print one row per thread. bwx12 is the runner of the 2026-11-15 investigation. bwx11 and bwx are older versions.
a process is one start of a benchmark binary.
one bwx12 process with the kernel sequence oldread, asmread, read_nop96, read_nop256, read_1pl.
one bwx12 process with the sequence oldread, read, asmread (cfwd) or asmread, read, oldread (crev).
the part L line, started from an idle machine, twice. It was added after the first numbers were seen. It is not part of the plan fixed before the run.
the inner loop of the benchmark that reads memory. On this page "kernel" means this loop. The operating system kernel is always written "Linux kernel".
portable C code with 16 running sums. Each load is followed by an add. Its name is `read` in the binary bw_old and `oldread` in the runner bwx12.
NEON intrinsics (C functions that map to Arm vector instructions), loads only. Its name is `read` in the binary bw_new and `read` in bwx12.
a hand-written load-only loop. It has the same 8 "ldp q" loads per 256 B as the new read kernel. "ldp q" is the Arm instruction that loads two 16-byte vector registers.
test loops of bwx12: the asmread loop with 96 or 256 no-operation instructions per 256 B, and a loop with one load per 64 B line.
the benchmark and its two binaries of 2026-11-13. bw_old was built from the old source, bw_new from the new source.
a text file that `rx.sh` reads as its input. Each line is `tag|arguments of the binary` and gives one process. The tag becomes the name of the csv file of that process.
a text file whose lines hold values separated by commas.

the file `/tmp/positron-perf.RUNNING`. The scripts of this test stop when it exists. The messages of rx.sh, `ra.sh` and go2.sh do not say what the file stands for. None of the scripts that test the file says who creates it. Since 2026-11-24 the message in line 20 of go.sh says what the file stands for: Jeremy or someone else is using CRB. Jeremy is another user of CRB. The page `go.sh.md` in the folder of go.sh (the explanation of go.sh) names the notes that say this. The facts sheet of the rerun says that another user creates it during a performance test [Ref7].
a line that go.sh or go2.sh prints with the time, the boot id, MemTotal, the load, the logins and the processes per user.
a random identifier that Linux creates at each start. Equal boot ids mean the same boot.
the usable memory that Linux reports, in kB.

the number of tasks that are runnable or wait for disk input and output, averaged by Linux over the last 1, 5 and 15 minutes (file `/proc/loadavg`). The fourth field of the file gives the tasks that are runnable now and the number of all tasks, for example `1/1013` [Ref5].
the number before the slash in the fourth field of `/proc/loadavg`: the processes and threads that are runnable at the moment of the reading [Ref5].
the column pcpu of the tool ps. It is the CPU time that a process has used, divided by the time since the process started [Ref8]. So it is an average over the life of the process.
a checksum. Two files with the same sha256 have the same content.
the number that a process returns when it ends. 0 means success. `launches.txt` writes it as `rc`.
the number that Linux gives to a process.
the CPUs on which Linux may run a process (its CPU affinity). A child process starts with the list of its parent [Ref6].
a Linux tool. `taskset -c 0-119 COMMAND` starts a command that may run on the CPUs 0 to 119 only. `taskset -cp PID` prints the CPU list of a running process.
Coordinated Universal Time. All times of the run are written in UTC.
